lawyer:
Abdul Quayum, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners. 
Mahbubey Alam with Mohammad Mostafa, Md Atiqul Haque, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Mahmood Alam (Md) and another ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Moklesur Rahman Bhuiya ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: This Rule was obtained by defendant Nos. 1 and 10 upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and decree dated 30-3-2000 passed by Additional District Judge, Court No. 2 at Barisal in Title Appeal No. 148 of 1996 affirming those dated 8-7-96 passed by Subordinate Judge, Court No. 1 in Title Suit No. 33 of 1995 in decreeing the suit.

2. Opposite party Nos. 1 to 3 and Mojibar Rahman, predecessor-in-interest of opposite party Nos. 4 to 13 as plaintiff instituted the suit for confirmation of their possession upon declaration of title by adverse possession in the suit land measuring about 0.092 acre of land comprised of holding No. 269/265 of No. 9 Hatkhola Ward of the Barisal Municipality fully described in the schedule to the plaint. Plaint case, in short is that the suit land originally belonged to Atul Behari Shaha and others, and in 1927 they orally settled the land with Hafizur Rahman Bhuiya alias Habu Khalifa, father of the plaintiffs at a rental of Taka 4 and put him into possession. Habu Khalifa possessed the land in his own right by raising dwelling house and living therein with his family up to 1965 when he died leaving the plaintiffs as his successors and heirs. In 1960, Habu Khalifa already orally gifted the land to the plaintiffs and delivered possession and the plaintiffs have since then been in possession of the suit land. After the death of Habu Khalifa, the plaintiffs constructed three more dwelling houses on the suit land. Plaintiffs also sank a deep tubewell in the land. One Hafez Noor Mohammad however got his name recorded in RS khatian No. 220 without the knowledge of the plaintiffs and SA Khatian was also prepared following the wrong entries of RS record. In fact, Hafez Noor Mohammad had got no right, title or possession in the suit land. As Hafez Noor Mohammad never asserted any sort of right or interest over the suit land, they did not need to take any steps. The plaintiffs have possessed the suit land for more than 70 years on assertions of their own right and title and adversely against and to the knowledge of all and such hostile possession have perfected their title in the suit land.

3. While they were thus owners in possession, on 29-5-95 defendant No.1 served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. On inquiry, they came to learn that after the death of Hafez Noor Mohammad, Nabijan Miah and Habib Box, and their sons Md Yousuf and Md Younus in collusion with the defendants created some papers in respect of the suit land. Then with such papers they got the land mutated in the names of the defendants in 1982-83 without any notice upon them. Now, they claim that the plaintiffs are their monthly tenants. After receipt of the above notice the plaintiffs were constrained to institute the suit.

4. Defendant Nos. 1 and 10 contested the suit by filing two separate written statements. Case of the defendant No. 1, in brief, is that both RS record and SA record of rights were correctly prepared in the name of Hafez Noor Mohammad as kolkorsha raiyat. Then, Hafez Noor Mohammad died leaving three sons. Matiur Rahman, Nurul Huda Miah and Nurul Hoq Miah, two daughters, Mabia Khatun and Rahima Khatun and a wife, Afserunnessa as his only heirs and legal representatives. Then Matiur Rahman and others agreed to sell the suit land to Habib Box and Nabijan Miah and executed a registered agreement on 28-8-56 and put them in possession in part performance of the agreement and ultimately, through their attorney Md Yousuf executed and registered a deed of sale on 7-7-57. At the time, Hafizur Rahman alias Habu Khalifa was a tenant in a portion of the suit land. Habib Box and Nabijan Miah got their names mutated on 20-6-75 and possessed the suit land by paying rents and municipal and other taxes. In Title Suit No. 253 of 1981 for partition, Nabijan Miah got 0.029 acre of land and the rest fell to the share of the heirs of Habib Box. Subsequently, defendant No. 1, his brothers and mother instituted Title Suit No. 67 of 1983 and defendant No.1 got 0.052 acre of land with the structures thereupon. Defendant No.1 thereupon got a separate Khatian No. 600 in respect of his share and he is living. Defendant Nos. 2 to 4 are possessing their share through monthly tenants, namely, Abdur Rahid (DW 2) and plaintiff No.1. Plaintiff No. 1 paid rents up to June, 1992 but thereafter stopped paying rents. Thereafter, serving a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 29-5-95 tenancy was terminated and instituted SCC Suit No. 10 of 1995 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge at Sadar in Barisal for eviction of plaintiff No.1.

5. The case of defendant No. 10 is same and identical with that of defendant No. 1. His further case is that plaintiff Nos. 3 and 4 are living in other portion of the suit land as monthly tenants under him. He claims that the deep tube well stands on his premises. He gave water connection to the tenants. He however lives outside the suit land.

6. On the pleading, various issues were framed. The plaintiffs examined three witnesses and adduced number of papers and documents, which were marked as exhibits No. 1 to 1(Ga), 2 to (Ka) and 3 while said defendants examined five witnesses and adduced exhibits No. K to Nio.

7. The trial Court decreed the suit as prayed for. On appeal, the Court of appeal dismissed the appeal and affirmed the decree of the trial Court by judgment and decree.

8. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner, submits that in the absence of proof of adverse possession in the suit land, the trial Court erred in law in decreeing the suit. He submits, in view of its own finding that the plaintiffs got land by way of settlement from the original rent receivers, the trial Court erred in law in decreeing the suit declaring title of the plaintiffs by adverse possession in that once entry into the land is established to be of lawful origin that never becomes adverse. Plaintiffs also failed to prove their possession hostile. The Court of appeal below fell in serious error in affirming such decree.

<u>9. He submits that the defendants proved their constructive possession through their tenants DW 2 Abdur Rashid and DW 3 Mofizur Rahaman and lease agreements exhibits 'Ta' and 'Tha' at least in a part of the suit land but the trial Court decreed the suit in respect of the entire suit land. In support, he cites the decisions in the cases of Golam Ilahi vs Md Waris Khan, 10 DLR (FC) 174; Abdur Kader vs Noor Mohammad, 36 DLR (AD) 261; Hazera Begum vs Rousahan Ara, 39 DLR (AD) 22; Achal Reddy vs Ramakrishna Reddiar; AIR 1990 (SC) 553=(1990) 4 SCC 706; Abdul Jalil Miah vs Niropama Ritchil, 49 DLR (AD) 61= 1997 BLD (AD) 63 and Salma Khatun vs Zilla Parishad 51 DLR (AD) 257.</u>

10. On the other hand, Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Counsel opposes the Rule submitting that the plaintiffs have proved their long, continuous and uninterrupted possession in the suit land since 1927 first by way of settlement by their father Hafizur Rahman Bhuiya alias Habu Khalifa and then, by the plaintiffs by open and overt enjoyment of the land against the whole world. Defendants totally failed to prove their possession in any part of the suit land as was found by the Courts below. Defendants also failed to prove their case of monthly tenancy. DW 2 and DW 3 are the tenants of the plaintiffs and the trial Court has correctly found that they were gained over during the proceeding of the suit, which would be evident, from exhibits 'Ta' and 'Tha'. He relies upon the decisions in the cases of Mahaprabhu Ram vs Gopal Ram 42 DLR (AD) 154; Jogendra Nath vs Amulya Chandra, 44 DLR (AD) 147 and Abdus Sattar vs Abdul Rahman, 44 DLR (AD) 100.

11. Only issue facing us is whether the Court of appeal below is well founded in affirming the decree of the trial Court in declaring the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land by adverse possession. To appreciate the conflicting submissions of the learned Counsels on adverse possession, we should first consider when adverse possession creates title and extinguishes a lawful title. We first see the decisions relied upon by the learned Counsels.

12. In Mst Golam Ilahi vs Md Waris Khan, 10 DLR (FC) 174 elder brother instituted the suit against his uterine sister for possession of his share in the property left by their mother on the ground that after her marriage in 1938 she lost her interest in the property under the custom. Sister resisted the claim pleading adverse possession on the basis of mutation in her name in 1915. The custom was that a daughter enjoyed limited interest in the property till marriage. According to the custom, the brother could not sue for possession before her marriage and the cause of action for possession would accrue only on such marriage, and since the suit was brought within twelve years of the marriage, the suit was found to be not barred by limitation and accordingly, decreed by the High Court at Lahore.

13. In dismissing the appeal preferred therefrom by the sister to the Federal Court of Pakistan, Mr Muhammad Munir, CJ writing the opinion on behalf of the Court was of the view that,

"Now the principle of law is that possession is not to be considered adverse if its origin can be referred to a lawful title whenever that is possible, because a person who claims to have entered into possession as a trespasser will be presumed not to have done so if at the time he so entered he had some lawful title to possession. This rule is an application of the wider principle which presumes against crime, wrong and fraud of every kind. Of course, the rule applies only where the facts are in doubt and not where the circumstances under which possession was assumed are known."

We find, main consideration weighed with the Court is as follows :

"There is no evidence whatsoever that before her marriage the appellant ever asserted that she had succeeded to the property as an owner with her brother so as to make it imperative for the latter to seek a declaration as to true nature of her possession.

14. In Abdul Kader vs Noor Mohammad. 36 DLR (AD) 261. the plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration of title and possession in the suit property and for further declaration that the compromise decree obtained in Title Suit No. 107 of 1966 was fraudulent, void and not binding upon them, and also for injunction, mainly on the basis of an agreement of sale from the original owner, Noor Mohammad Bepari. Three sets of defendants opposed the claims of the plaintiffs. Defendant No. 1 claimed to have acquired the suit land by successive settlements from the original owner and also on the aforesaid compromise decree. Various suits instituted earlier for cancellation of the compromise decree failed. Defendant Nos. 3 to 5 claimed through successive purchases from the said owner while defendant No. 6, the Government, claimed to have requisitioned the suit property on 23-7-47 and allotted it to class-IV employees. In affirming the decision of the Courts below of dismissal of the suit, Mr Fazle Munim CJ, was of the view. "In the present case there is no evidence to show that the plaintiff-appellants ever claimed any title to the suit property on adverse possession, nor when their possession became hostile to Noor Mohammad Bepari the owner of the suit property. Also they never asserted hostile title against him. On the contrary, it is admitted by the appellants that they entered the suit premises with the permission of the owner who, however, allowed it to be requisitioned by the Government for the accommodation of Government employees. From the Government papers produced by the learned Additional Attorney-General, it is seen that the suit premises are still under requisition. Moreover, the present suit is not for declaration of plaintiff’s title by adverse possession, but for declaration that the compromise decree obtained by some of the respondents in Title Suit No. 107 of 1966 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is fraudulent, void and not binding upon them. In this suit, therefore, plaintiff-appellants are not entitled to any relief whatsoever."

15. In Hazera Begum vs Roushan Ara. 39 DLR (AD) 22 the suit of the plaintiffs for partition on declaration of title in respect of their share was resisted by the defendants pleading adverse possession. All the Courts found that the property was joint and the plaintiff’s co-sharers, and the defendants failed to prove ouster or exclusion of the plaintiffs from possession of the property. Accordingly, the suit was decreed and the Appellate Division finally affirmed the decree.

16. In the Secretary of State for India vs Debendra Lal Khan. 38 CWN 285. the Privy Council was of the view.

"It is sufficient that the possession should be overt and without any attempt at concealment, so that the person against whom time is running out, if he exercise due vigilance, to be aware of what is happening."

17. In Mahaprabhu Ram vs Gopal Ram. 42 DLR (AD) 154. the plaintiff sought for partition to the extent of eight annas share by way of inheritance from his father, which was resisted by his first cousins saying that the plaintiff had no right, title or possession in the suit land. Before the Appellate Division, title was claimed by adverse possession as well. In dispelling such claim and in affirming the dismissal of the suit, Mr Mostafa Kamal, J as his Lordship then was, took the view.

"The appellant never prayed for partition on the basis that he or his predecessor acquired title to the suit property by adverse possession. Title by adverse possession has to be specifically pleaded and proved. The appellant's case was one of acquisition of title by settlement. The trial Court found that the case of settlement has not been proved, but it conferred title on the appellant on a gratuitous finding of adverse possession in his favour, unwarranted by pleadings. This gratuitous conferment of title was uncalled for in a suit for partition where the plaintiffs’ claim of title is to be looked into incidentally. If the precise title to which he lays his claim is not supported by the evidence on record, the Court cannot find out another source of title for the plaintiff by way of gratuitous relief."

18. In Achal Reddy vs Ramakrishan Reddiar, AIR 1990 (SC) 553= (1990) 4 SCC 706, plaintiff instituted the suit for recovery of possession from a trespasser. Suit was filed within twelve years of dispossession. The plaintiff claimed to have entered into possession on the basis of an arrangement with Muthukrishna Reddi who, as an heir of Varada Reddi, got a decree for specific performance of an agreement. The decree became final but not executed. Arrangement was made after the decree. Dasu Reddy, as owner of the land executed the agreement dated July 10, 1946 to transfer the land to Varada Reddy. The trespasser claimed that said Muthukrishna Reddi orally transferred the land to him. The Supreme Court of India confirmed the decree of the letters patent bench of the High Court for possession on the following view,

"The parties are concluded by the finding of the Division Bench that the transaction of July 10, 1946 between Dasu Reddi and Varada Reddi is only an agreement for sale and not an oral sale of the property. If that be so the possession of Varada Reddi in pursuance of such an agreement of sale and in the expectation that there would be a complete divestiture of all the rights of the owner in his favour on execution of a regular sale deed, until the execution of the sale deed, was only possession on behalf of Dasu Reddi. Such possession having been within a period of 12 years prior to the present suit, the plaintiff succeeds in having established the possession of his predecessor-in-interest within 12 years prior to the date of the suit. The plaintiff is, therefore, entitled to a decree in his favour. The decision of the letters patent bench of the High Court is correct and we confirm the same. The appeal is accordingly dismissed with costs."

19. In the course of judgment, the Court also considered the nature of possession on the basis of a contract of sale. The following ratio decidendi for the judgment would be of immense help to answer the issue of adverse possession as raised in the case at hand,

"In the case of an executory contract of sale where the transferee is put in possession of the property in pursuance of the agreement of sale and where the parties contemplate the execution of a regular registered sale deed the animus of the purchaser throughout is that he is in possession of the property belonging to the vendor and that the former's title has to be perfected by a duly executed registered deed of sale under which the vendor has to pass on and convey his title. The purchaser's possession in such cases is of a derivative character and in clear recognition of and in acknowledgement of the title of the vendor. The position is different in the case where in pursuance of an oral transfer or a deed of transfer not registered the owner of a property transfers the property and puts the transferee in possession with the clear animus and on the distinct understanding that from that time onwards he shall have no right or title to the property. In such a case the owner of the property does not retain any vestige of right in regard to the property and his mental attitude towards the property is that it has ceased to belong to him altogether. The transferee after getting into possession retains the same with clean animus that he has become the absolute owner of the property and in complete negation of any right or title of the transferor, his enjoyment solely as owner in his right and not derivatively or in recognition of the title of any person. So far as the vendor is concerned both in mind and actual conduct, there is a total divestiture of all the right, title and interest in the property. This applies only in a case where there is a clear manifestation of the intention of the owner to divest himself of the right over the property. On the other hand, in the case of an executory contract the possession of the transferee until the date of registration of the conveyance is permissive or derivative and in law is deemed to be on behalf of the owner himself."

20. Abdul Jalil Miah vs Niropama Ritchil, 49 DLR (AD) 61=1997 BLD (AD) 63 arises out of a suit for declaration of title by adverse possession. The plaintiff claimed to have entered into possession in 1963 on the basis of an agreement of sale executed by defendant No. 1 and continued to be in such possession adversely against the world. Defendant No.2 opposed the claim on the basis of decree of title she obtained by way of inheritance from her mother against defendant No. 1 who happened to be her father. Her further case is that she let the suit premises to the plaintiff on a monthly lease and he paid rent to her up to the middle of 1975. The trial Court found that defendant No. 1 had no saleable interest in the suit land and so possession of the plaintiff could not be construed as lawful, which was continuous since 1963 within the knowledge of defendant No. 2 rightful owner and that the plaintiff acquired a good title by adverse possession. The Appellate Division however found the period of adverse possession falls short by three years to mature into a good title. In affirming the decision of this Division in dismissing the suit, Mr BB Roy Chowdhury, J was of the following view.

"when the plaintiff after getting into possession retains the same with clean animus that he has become the absolute owner of the property in complete negation of any right or title of the true owner thereof i.e. defendant No. 2, his enjoyment would be solely in assertion of hostile title.

"In order to claim title by adverse possession it is incumbent upon a person to prove that he has been in continuous possession of the disputed property over the statutory period of 12 years in assertion of his hostile which the plaintiff has failed to prove."

21. Jogendra Nath vs Amulya Chandra, 44 DLR (AD) 147 arises out of a suit for partition. The plaintiff claimed partition on the basis of a will but the defendants opposed the claim by adverse possession. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the conclusion that the plaintiff’s title was extinguished by adverse possession of the uncles of the plaintiff and their transferees. This Division affirmed the decision. In confirming the decision of this Division, the Appellate Division was of the view.

"Admittedly, the uncles of the plaintiff and their transferees including the predecessor of the contesting defendant have been in possession of the suit land contrary to the provisions of the will Exhibit 1 for more than 12 years and the executor and the plaintiff himself (on attainment of majority) stood by until the suit was filed in 1968. Thus it cannot be said that the finding as to adverse possession was wrongly made."

22. In Abdus Sattar vs Abdul Rahman, 44 DLR (AD) 100, the suit was instituted for declaration of title and recovery of possession in respect of four annas share by way of settlement was resisted by the defendants who got admittedly twelve annas share of the holding by settlement but claiming possession in entire 16 annas of the holding for over the period of 35 years. Accepting the adverse possession of the defendants in respect of said four annas share, this Division reversed the concurrent decree of the Courts below and dismissed the suit. On the following view, the Appellate Division confirmed the decision of this Division,

"there is no evidence whatsoever that during this long period any of the landlords, either Ramanath Ghosh Estate or Gobinda Jieu, made any demand or raised any objection with regard to the defendant's possession of the suit land. There is no material or circumstance on record to show that the defendants possessed the suit land in any manner except in assertion of their own right against all others. In view of the findings of fact made even by the Courts below, we find it impossible to hold that the defendants were in possession of the suit land on behalf of their landords negating the doctrine "Tenant stealing for the landlord."

<u>23. In Salma Khatun vs Zilla Parishad, 51 DLR (AD) 257 the plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration of title on the basis of successive transfers from one Noor Hossain who got settlement from the Zilla Parishad. SA record of rights stands in the name of said Noor Hossain. The Zilla Parishad resisted the claim saying that they never settled the land with Noor Hossain nor received any rent from him. Plaintiff created papers to grab the property of Zilla Parishad. Trial Court decreed the suit. But this Division dismissed the suit. The Appellate Division affirmed the decision of this Division, on the view,</u>

<u>" ... the plaintiffs could not file any paper to show the alleged raiyati right of Noor Hossain on the basis of settlement or lease taken from defendant No. 1. The High Court Division was well founded in law in holding that under the circumstances the plaintiffs have established a case of possession but not of title. When they are in possession claiming raiyati settlement they cannot set up adverse possession either. They are not entitled to a declaration of title."</u>

24. Adverse possession is a mixed question of fact and law, in the sense. that the fact of adverse possession is to be gathered from surrounding circumstances and then, to decide whether such possession creates title in favour of the person in such possession. What constitutes adverse possession in law is also now well settled by the pronouncements of highest judicial authorities. Besides the above cases, in Secy of State for India in Council vs Debendra Lal Khan, (1933) 61 IA 78: 1934 All LJ 153 (PC) the Privy Council laid down that it is sufficient that the possession must be overt and without any attempt at concealment so that the person against whom time is running out if he exercises due vigilance, to be aware of what is happening and if the rights of the Crown have been openly usurped it cannot be heard to plead that the fact was not to its notice. In P Lakshmi Reddy vs Lakshmi Reddy, AIR 1957 (SC) 314, the Supreme Court of India observed that it should be nec vi, nee clam, nec preeario-that is, the possession required must be adequate in continuity, in publicity and in extent to show that it is possession adverse to the competitor. In Annasaheb Bapusaheb Patil vs Balwant, (1995) 2 SCC 543; AIR 1995 (SC) 895 it again observed that a claim of adverse possession being a hostile assertion involving expressly or impliedly in denial of the title of true owner, the burden is always on the person who asserts such a claim to prove by clear and unequivocal evidence that his possession was hostile to the real owner and in deciding such claim, the Courts must have regard to the animus of the person doing those acts. Once adverse possession for over the statutory period of limitation is established, the person in such possession becomes entitled to a decree since it is one of the accepted modes of acquisition of title in property.

25. Turning to the facts of the case at hand, we find the plaintiffs claim that in 1927, Atul Behari Saha and others, admitted rent receivers settled the suit land orally with their father, Hajizur Rahman, Habu Khalifa at a rental of Taka 4.00 and handed over possession to him, and after he entered into the land, he erected a house and started living with his family therein. He admittedly lived there up to 1965. During his lifetime, in 1960 he already gifted the suit land to the plaintiffs. Plaintiffs also erected 3 more houses on the suit land. On 29-5-1995, they received a legal notice issued on behalf of the defendant No. 1 and after inquiry; they came to know for the first time that the defendants created some forged, antedated and collusive papers in the names of Habib Box and Nabijan Mia through their sons, Yousuf and Younus as attorney.

26. Further case of the plaintiffs is that their father was in the nature of humble disposition, he did not care to know about the record of rights nor he paid any rents. RS and SA khatians though record the name of Hajji Noor Mohammed but neither he nor his any heirs ever asserted any claim whatsover over the suit land. Nor even the rent receivers or anybody on their behalf claimed any interest in the suit land. Defendants also did not claim any interest over the suit land till the issue of the legal notice in 1995. Consequently, the plaintiffs continued to possess and enjoy the suit land since 1927 on assertion of their own rights and interest continuously, openly, overtly, and adversely against the world including the defendants. Such adverse possession for more than 70 years has perfected their title in the suit land.

27. On the other hand, defendant Nos. I and 10 claims that Hajji Noor Mohammed took settlement from said Atul Behari Saha and others and RS and SA record of rights were correctly prepared in his names. Then, Nsbijan Mia and Habib Box purchased the suit land from the heirs of said Hajji Noor Mohammed by registered deed dated 7-7-57 and go their names mutated in mutation case No. 107(II) K.T/74-75 on 20-6-75. By way of a compromise decree in Title Suit No. 253 of 1981 dated 4-9-82 Nabijan Mia got 0.029 acre of the suit land and in other compromise decree dated 17-1-84 passed in. Title Suit No. 67 of 1983 defendant No.1 got the rest of the suit land measuring about 0.052 acre. Defendant No. 1 got the land mutated in his Khatain No. 600.

28. Their further case is when Nabijan Mia and Habib Box purchased. Habu Khalifa, father of the plaintiffs was living in the suit land as a monthly tenant. Now, plaintiff No. 1 lives in a part as a monthly tenant under defendant No. 1 while plaintiffs Nos. 2 to 4 live in other parts of the suit land as monthly tenants under defendant No. 10. When they stopped payment of rents, the tenancy was terminated by service of a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property, Act and SCC suit No. 1 of 1995 was also instituted for ejectment.

29. We have again placed the pleadings a bit detail before us. On the pleadings, one fact is admitted by the defendants that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land at least since 1956, according to defendants. But there is not an iota of evidence on record to show anybody else possessed the suit land from prior to 1956 up to 1927 save and except Habu Khalifa. Presumption, if any, arising out of RS record of rights and SA record of rights prepared on the previous record was washed away by long, open and overt continuous possession of Habu Khalifa. Trial Court could not find any evidence oral or documentary whatsoever on record to support such record of rights, we find correctly. It has accordingly, held that those record of rights were wrong.

30. Secondly, the defendants now admit that they do not physically possess the suit land. But all their attempts to prove constructive possession in the suit land first through Habu Khalifa and then, through the plaintiffs as tenants also fall through for want of evidence. They failed to adduce any evidence whatsoever even in support of assertion of possession in the suit land before 29-5-95. They examined DW 2 Abdur Rashid and DW 3 Mofizur Rahman to prove them as tenants under them and to prove their constructive possession through them. They also adduced two lease agreements alleged to have been executed by DW 2 and DW 3 exhibits 'Ta' and 'Tha'. They claim that they are living in two houses of the suit land as tenants under defendants. Both the documents appear to be executed on 28-8- 95 after the institution of the suit on 23-6-95. Similarly, DW 5, Saidul Islam was examined to prove that he got the deep tubewell sunk on the suit land on the basis of an agreement, exhibit 'Nio', this document was also executed during the pendency of the suit. All these papers only testify to support the suggestion of the plaintiffs that the DW 2 and DW 3 who were their tenants were gained over by the defendants after the suit. Therefore, the Court of appeal below did not commit any error in affirming the finding of the trial Court that the defendants failed to prove the plaintiffs possess the suit land as tenants.

31. On elaborate consideration, the trial Court has held that the documents as adduced by the defendants in support of their title were mere paper transaction. The decrees as mentioned hereinbefore were also created by fraud and forgery. It has clearly found that no heir of Hajji Noor Mohammed executed the deed dated 7-7-57, exhibit 'Ga'. In order to decide the issue facing us, we find no need to go into detail on such findings. What we find is that the Courts below did not commit any error in excluding those documents in deciding the issue.

<u>32. On the evidence on record, and in the circumstances of the case, the trial Court has come to a conclusion that the plaintiffs have acquired right and title in the suit land first by settlement and then, by way of adverse possession. By independent consideration, the Court of appeal below appears to have affirmed such finding.</u>

<u>33. Mr Quayum challenges this conclusion and the decree passed upon such conclusion in submitting that once possession lawfully i.e. by way of settlement commences, such possession can never transform into an adverse possession. He heavily relies upon the decisions in the cases of Most Golam Ilahi vs Md Waris Khan and Salma Khatun vs Zilla Parishad. The principle he wants to stand on is a very well-known standard, namely, the possession to become adverse must have commenced in wrong and maintained against right. But this is not the only and conclusive criterion for adverse possession as we have found in the above cases. In Achal Reddy vs Ramakrishna Reddiar; the Supreme Court of India has observed that where a transferee enters either on the basis. of an oral transfer or a deed of transfer into possession of a property and retains such possession with a clean animus that he has become the absolute owner of the property and in complete negation of any right or title of the transferor, his enjoyment is solely as owner in his right and not derivatively or in recognition of the title of any person. Such possession must be held to be adverse and if he continuously possesses for the statutory period of 12 years and if the true owner fails to institute a suit for possession, then the title of such true owner under section 28 of the Limitation Act becomes extinguished. Consequently, the person in such possession becomes entitled to own the property as his own.</u>

34. As stated above, in 1927 Habu Khalifa, father of the plaintiffs, entered into possession of the suit land on the basis of an oral settlement, and possessed till his death in 1965 with clean animus, that he became the absolute owner of the suit land and in complete negation of any right or title of any person including the rent receivers and then, on his death the plaintiffs have similarly been continuing and enjoying their possession on assertion of their own right and title overtly and openly and without any attempt at concealment. Such long continuous possession with clean animus of an absolute owner must be held to be hostile to anybody including the defendants. To make such possession hostile, and consequently, adverse the plaintiffs were never required to announce/publicise their hostility by beat of drums.

35. In view of the above legal position, the findings of the trial Court that the plaintiffs have acquired right and title in the suit land by long, continuous and overt possession for more than 70 years are well founded. So, the Court of appeal below did not commit any error of law or procedure in affirming the decree of the trial Court upon such conclusion by the impugned judgment and decree, which have not resulted in any failure of Justice.

36. In the result, this Rule is discharged without however any order as to costs. Impugned judgment and decree affirming those of the trial Court are hereby confirmed.

Send down the records at once.

End.
